say: Okay, quick question. Drop almost any solid into its own liquid, and it sinks. Solid wax in melted wax? Sinks. But ice? Ice floats. And that's actually super weird.
Normally, when stuff gets colder, its molecules huddle closer together. Tighter packing means heavier for its size. So the solid should sink. Makes sense, right?
Well, water plays by different rules. Each molecule is one oxygen and two hydrogens, and they stick to their neighbors with something called hydrogen bonds.
In liquid water, those bonds snap and re-form constantly. It's basically a crowded dance floor. Molecules bumping around, packed pretty close.
But when water freezes, the bonds lock into a hexagon pattern, with empty space in the middle of every ring. Fun fact, that's also why snowflakes have six sides.
All that empty space makes ice about nine percent less dense than liquid water. Lighter for its size. So, it floats. Simple as that.
And it gets weirder. Water is actually heaviest at about four degrees Celsius. So in winter, the coldest water rises to the top of a lake, and freezes there first.
That lid of ice keeps the water underneath from freezing solid, so fish can survive the whole winter down there. If ice sank? Lakes would freeze from the bottom up.
